cues.text: Let us turn now to algorithmic profiling and targeted advertising.
Begin with the core idea.
Profiling uses data to evaluate or predict aspects of a person.
Notice the two verbs there: evaluate and predict.
A profile is not simply a record of what someone did.
It is a judgement or a forecast about who that person is, what they like, or what they are likely to do next.
Consider how this works in practice.
A recommender system may rank content based on four things: past engagement, similarities among users, estimated relevance, and business objectives.
Past engagement means what you have previously clicked, watched or reacted to.
Similarities among users means the system notices that people who behave like you tended to enjoy certain things, and so it offers you those things too.
Estimated relevance is the system's own calculation of how well an item fits you.
And business objectives remind us that the ranking is not neutral; the organisation running the platform has goals of its own, and those goals shape what you see.
A classifier is a different tool.
A classifier may infer interests or risk categories.

In other words, it sorts people into groups, such as people interested in a particular topic, or people judged to fall into a certain risk category, even when the person never stated that information directly.
Now, targeted advertising.
The source gives us both sides.
On the positive side, targeted advertising can improve relevance and finance services.
People may see advertisements that actually matter to them, and the revenue helps pay for services.
On the negative side, it may expose sensitive interests, reinforce stereotypes, exclude groups, or manipulate choices.
Let me take those four harms one at a time.
Exposing sensitive interests means that inferences about a person may reveal things they would prefer to keep private.
Reinforcing stereotypes means the system may treat people according to assumed group traits.
Excluding groups means some people may never even see certain opportunities or offers.
And manipulating choices means that the targeting may steer decisions rather than inform them.
As you study this, ask yourself who the parties are: the individual, the advertiser, and the platform.
Each has different interests, and those interests can conflict.
Next, engagement metrics.
These include clicks, comments, shares, watch time and reactions.
Platforms use them to measure whether content is succeeding.
But here is the central warning.
Optimising a proxy rather than a real goal can amplify outrage or controversy.
A proxy is a stand-in measure.
Clicks are a stand-in for value or interest, but they are not the same thing as genuine benefit to the user.
If a system is rewarded for engagement, it may promote whatever provokes the strongest reaction.
The source adds an important qualification: negative interactions may be counted as engagement depending on model design.
So an angry comment can count just as much as an approving one, if the model is built that way.
Notice the qualification, depending on model design.
It is not true of every system, but it is a risk.
The source then turns to algorithmic bias.
It may arise from several places: training data, objective functions, feature selection, feedback loops, deployment contexts and moderation rules.
Let me go through each.
Training data is the historical information the model learns from; if it reflects past unfairness or gaps, the model can learn them.
The objective function is what the model is told to optimise.
Feature selection is the choice of which inputs the model uses.
Feedback loops, which we will see in the diagram in a moment, are cases where the model's outputs shape future data.
Deployment contexts means that a model used in a setting different from the one it was designed for may behave unfairly.
And moderation rules, the policies that govern what content is allowed or demoted, can also introduce bias.
Then comes a vital caution: an apparent correlation is not proof of fairness or causation.
Just because two things move together does not mean one causes the other, and it does not mean the outcome is fair.
Now look at the accompanying diagram, which is a simple loop.
It reads: Behaviour, then collected signals, then profile or ranking, then exposure.
From exposure, an arrow returns upward to behaviour, and it is labelled the feedback loop.
Walk through it in order.
First, a person behaves: they click, watch or react.
Second, the system collects signals from that behaviour.
Third, those signals build a profile or produce a ranking.
Fourth, the person is exposed to content or advertising according to that profile.
Then the loop closes: what the person is exposed to influences their next behaviour, which produces new signals, and the cycle repeats.
This is why biases can compound.
If the first ranking is skewed, the exposure is skewed, the resulting behaviour is skewed, and the next ranking inherits that skew.
This leads naturally to two concepts that are often confused.
An echo chamber reinforces similar views through social choices and content selection.
Think of the role played by who you follow, who you engage with, and what is selected for you.
A filter bubble, by contrast, describes personalised exposure that can limit diversity.
The distinction is one of emphasis: the echo chamber stresses social choices together with content selection, while the filter bubble stresses personalisation by the system.
The source is careful to add that neither is inevitable for every user.
Do not assume that everyone is trapped in one.
Then there is political microtargeting.
This may exploit psychological vulnerabilities and reduce transparent public deliberation, especially when messages differ by audience without meaningful scrutiny.
Picture different groups receiving different political messages, with no one able to compare them or challenge them.
Public debate depends on shared visibility of what is being claimed, and when that is lost, accountability suffers.
So how should we reason about all this?
The source states that the benefits of advertising must be weighed against autonomy, fairness, informed choice and democratic integrity.
This is a balancing exercise.
On one side are relevance and the financing of services.
On the other are the person's ability to make their own decisions, equal and fair treatment, choices made with real understanding, and the health of democratic processes.
Finally, the source lists measures that may help: transparency reports, ad libraries, privacy-preserving measurement, opt-outs and independent audits.
Transparency reports disclose how a platform operates.
Ad libraries make advertisements publicly viewable.
Privacy-preserving measurement evaluates advertising performance while protecting personal data.
Opt-outs let individuals decline.
Independent audits allow outside parties to examine systems.
Notice the closing qualification: these may help, depending on law and design.
They are not guaranteed solutions, and whether any of them is required is a question of the applicable law, not of ethics alone.
